title: Piano Concerto No. 1 in B-flat minor
hook: The concerto its first listener tore apart, with an opening tune that never comes back.

painting.title: The Rooks Have Returned
painting.pairingNote: Painted by a Moscow teacher a few years before the concerto, the first thaw of a Russian spring; the finale is built on a Ukrainian song that calls the spring in.

facts: Tchaikovsky wrote the concerto in Moscow between November 1874 and February 1875, while he was teaching at the Moscow Conservatory.

On Christmas Eve 1874 he played it to Nikolai Rubinstein, the head of the conservatory, who he hoped would perform it. Rubinstein tore it apart and demanded changes. Tchaikovsky, by his own account, refused to change a single note. Rubinstein later became one of the concerto’s champions.

The first performance was given far from Russia, in Boston, on 25 October 1875, by the German pianist Hans von Bülow, to whom the concerto is dedicated. Tchaikovsky revised it in 1879 and again in 1888; the 1888 version is the one usually played.
Folk songs run through it: a tune Tchaikovsky heard from blind street musicians at a market in Kamianka, in Ukraine (I), a light French song (II) and a Ukrainian song to greet the spring (III).
bigPicture.inOneLine: a giant introduction and a jumpy folk tune (I), a gentle pastoral with a fast scherzo in the middle (II), a whirling dance that ends in a blaze (III).

movements.heading: Allegro non troppo e molto maestoso – Allegro con spirito
movements.tempo: Allegro non troppo e molto maestoso – Allegro con spirito
movements.summary: It opens with one of the best-known tunes in classical music, played by the strings while the piano pounds out huge chords. Then the tune disappears for good. The rest of the movement, in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], is built on a skittish Ukrainian folk tune and a gentler, more consoling melody, with three [[cadenza|cadenza]]s for the piano.

mainIdeas.name: The horn call
mainIdeas.description: four falling notes on the horns, loud, at the very start.

mainIdeas.name: The big tune
mainIdeas.description: a broad, sweeping melody in D-flat major, first in the violins and cellos.

mainIdeas.name: The folk tune
mainIdeas.description: quick, jumpy and nervous, first in the piano, in B-flat minor.

mainIdeas.name: The consoling theme
mainIdeas.description: smooth and warm, in the strings, over a held bass note.

stops.hear: Four loud, falling notes on the horns, then crashing chords
stops.happening: The opening call, in B-flat minor

stops.hear: Violins and cellos sweep into the big tune; the piano pounds huge chords up and down the keyboard against it
stops.happening: The introduction’s famous theme, in D-flat major

stops.hear: The piano plays the big tune itself, then breaks into a short, free solo
stops.happening: The second statement, and a first [[cadenza|cadenza]]

stops.hear: The strings take the tune once more, at full strength, with sweeping piano runs around it
stops.happening: The third and last time we hear it

stops.hear: The music sinks and goes quiet
stops.happening: The introduction fades away. The big tune never returns

stops.hear: The piano starts a quick, jumpy, slightly limping tune
stops.happening: The folk tune, in B-flat minor. The [[exposition|exposition]] proper begins

stops.hear: The woodwinds, softly, play a calmer, gentler melody; the piano answers
The strings play a smooth, consoling melody over a held low note
stops.happening: The consoling theme, in A-flat major, over a [[pedal-note|pedal note]]

stops.hear: The woodwind melody returns, driven by surging piano runs, up to a stormy climax; then a short piano solo
stops.happening: The climax of the exposition and a brief cadenza

stops.hear: Ominous, building phrases; piano octaves; fragments of the themes in new keys, a soft drum roll underneath
The jumpy folk tune returns, shorter
The orchestra drops out; the piano alone plays a long, elaborate solo, by turns stormy and quiet
The orchestra comes back with the consoling theme, now in B-flat major
stops.happening: The closing section, in the major

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Everything builds to a short, triumphant ending

notice: The big tune is heard only three times, all in the first three minutes. After that the concerto never mentions it again.
In the development, listen for a soft, steady drum roll on one low note under the music, like a held breath.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Argerich played the concerto live in Munich in February 1980 with Kirill Kondrashin, who had conducted Van Cliburn’s prize-winning performance of the same concerto in Moscow in 1958. Kondrashin died in 1981, and Philips first released this performance in 1982 as a tribute to him. On the Spotify album the Tchaikovsky is tracks 4–6, after Rachmaninoff’s Third Concerto.

movements.heading: Andantino semplice – Prestissimo – Tempo I
movements.summary: A gentle, pastoral movement with a surprise in the middle. A flute sings a simple tune over plucked strings, and the piano repeats it. Then the music suddenly races: a light, fast [[scherzo|scherzo]], built on a popular French song. At the end the gentle tune returns.

mainIdeas.name: The flute tune
mainIdeas.description: simple, slow and rocking, in D-flat major.

mainIdeas.name: The French song
mainIdeas.description: a light, skipping melody. Its words mean “One must have fun, dance and laugh”.

stops.hear: Soft, plucked strings
A flute plays a simple, gentle tune
The piano repeats the tune, a little changed
The tune passes between piano and woodwinds; the piano decorates it
Suddenly very fast: the piano flickers and flutters
Under the piano’s flutter, a light, skipping tune appears in the orchestra
stops.happening: The French song “Il faut s’amuser, danser et rire”

stops.hear: A rippling run on the piano; the music slows
The gentle tune returns
stops.happening: The main theme comes back (*Tempo I*)

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Quiet chords; the movement ends very softly

notice: Compare the flute and the piano in the first minute. Same tune, two colours.

movements.heading: Allegro con fuoco
movements.summary: A fast, stamping dance in three beats, built on a Ukrainian song that greets the spring. Against it Tchaikovsky sets a broad, singing melody. The two alternate, like a [[rondo|rondo]], and at the end the singing melody returns in the full orchestra, now in B-flat major, before a dash to the finish.

mainIdeas.name: The spring dance
mainIdeas.description: quick, accented, in three beats, first in the piano.

mainIdeas.name: The broad melody
mainIdeas.description: a long, warm tune in the strings, related to a Russian folk song.

stops.hear: A short, quiet start in the orchestra; then the piano launches a quick, stamping dance
stops.happening: Theme 1, the Ukrainian spring song, in B-flat minor

stops.hear: The orchestra takes the dance; the piano answers with sharp chords
stops.happening: The dance passes back and forth

stops.hear: The strings play a broad, warm melody
The piano takes up the melody in big chords
The dance returns and is passed around; brilliant piano runs
The broad melody returns, in a new key
The music gathers itself; a long build, louder and louder
The whole orchestra plays the broad melody at full power in B-flat major; the piano crashes out chords
stops.happening: *Molto meno mosso*: the big tune as the climax, in [[tutti|tutti]]

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: Racing piano octaves and closing chords

notice: The finale’s broad melody arrives three times. Notice how it grows each time, until the last statement fills the whole orchestra.
The concerto began in B-flat minor and ends in B-flat major.

threads.title: Folk songs
threads.body: Each movement borrows a popular tune: a song of Ukrainian street musicians, a French song and a Ukrainian spring song.

threads.title: The vanishing tune
threads.body: The most famous melody in the concerto is used only in the introduction. Analysts have found its shapes hidden in the themes of all three movements.

threads.title: Piano against orchestra
threads.body: Here the soloist really does fight: huge chords against the full orchestra, and three cadenzas in the first movement alone.
